import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import os

working_dir = os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "working")
os.makedirs(working_dir, exist_ok=True)

try:
    experiment_data = np.load(
        os.path.join(working_dir, "experiment_data.npy"), allow_pickle=True
    ).item()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error loading experiment data: {e}")
    experiment_data = {}

ds_key = "llama3_advbench_alpaca"
data = experiment_data.get(ds_key, {})

# Plot 1: Probe accuracy per layer with baselines
try:
    val_metrics = data["metrics"]["val"]
    train_metrics = data["metrics"]["train"]
    layers = [m["layer"] for m in val_metrics]
    val_accs = [m["acc"] for m in val_metrics]
    rand_accs = [m["random"] for m in val_metrics]
    shuf_accs = [m["shuffled"] for m in val_metrics]
    train_accs = [m["acc"] for m in train_metrics]

    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
    plt.plot(layers, val_accs, "o-", label="Diff-of-means (val)")
    plt.plot(layers, rand_accs, "s--", label="Random direction (val)")
    plt.plot(layers, shuf_accs, "^--", label="Shuffled labels (val)")
    plt.xlabel("Layer")
    plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
    plt.title(
        "Harmfulness Probe Accuracy per Layer\nDataset: AdvBench (harmful) vs Alpaca (benign), Model: Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
    )
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, f"{ds_key}_probe_accuracy_baselines.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot1: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 2: Train vs Val accuracy per layer
try:
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
    plt.plot(layers, train_accs, "o-", label="Train")
    plt.plot(layers, val_accs, "s-", label="Validation")
    plt.xlabel("Layer")
    plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
    plt.title(
        "Train vs Validation Probe Accuracy per Layer\nDataset: AdvBench/Alpaca, Model: Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
    )
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, f"{ds_key}_train_val_accuracy.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot2: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 3: Loss per layer
try:
    train_losses = [m["loss"] for m in data["losses"]["train"]]
    val_losses = [m["loss"] for m in data["losses"]["val"]]
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
    plt.plot(layers, train_losses, "o-", label="Train Loss (1 - acc)")
    plt.plot(layers, val_losses, "s-", label="Val Loss (1 - acc)")
    plt.xlabel("Layer")
    plt.ylabel("Loss (1 - accuracy)")
    plt.title(
        "Probe Loss per Layer\nDataset: AdvBench/Alpaca, Model: Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
    )
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, f"{ds_key}_loss_per_layer.png"), bbox_inches="tight"
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot3: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 4: Confusion matrix at best layer
try:
    preds = np.array(data["predictions"])
    gts = np.array(data["ground_truth"])
    best_layer = data.get("best_layer", "N/A")
    cm = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    for t, p in zip(gts, preds):
        cm[int(t), int(p)] += 1

    plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
    plt.imshow(cm, cmap="Blues")
    plt.colorbar()
    for i in range(2):
        for j in range(2):
            plt.text(
                j,
                i,
                str(cm[i, j]),
                ha="center",
                va="center",
                color="black",
                fontsize=14,
            )
    plt.xticks([0, 1], ["Benign", "Harmful"])
    plt.yticks([0, 1], ["Benign", "Harmful"])
    plt.xlabel("Predicted")
    plt.ylabel("Ground Truth")
    plt.title(
        f"Confusion Matrix at Best Layer ({best_layer})\nDataset: AdvBench/Alpaca, Model: Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
    )
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, f"{ds_key}_confusion_matrix_best_layer.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot4: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 5: Direction norm per layer
try:
    per_layer = data.get("per_layer", {})
    ls = sorted(per_layer.keys())
    norms = [per_layer[L]["direction_norm"] for L in ls]
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
    plt.plot(ls, norms, "o-", color="purple")
    plt.xlabel("Layer")
    plt.ylabel("||mu_harmful - mu_benign||")
    plt.title(
        "Mean-Difference Direction Norm per Layer\nDataset: AdvBench/Alpaca, Model: Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
    )
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, f"{ds_key}_direction_norm_per_layer.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot5: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Print evaluation metric
try:
    print(f"Best layer: {data.get('best_layer')}")
    print(
        f"Harmfulness direction probe accuracy: {data.get('harmfulness_direction_probe_accuracy'):.4f}"
    )
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error printing metric: {e}")

import os
import numpy as np

working_dir = os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "working")
experiment_data = np.load(
    os.path.join(working_dir, "experiment_data.npy"), allow_pickle=True
).item()

for dataset_name, data in experiment_data.items():
    print(f"Dataset: {dataset_name}")

    best_layer = data.get("best_layer", None)
    best_probe_acc = data.get("harmfulness_direction_probe_accuracy", None)

    per_layer = data.get("per_layer", {})

    if per_layer:
        # Find best layer by val accuracy
        best_L = max(per_layer.keys(), key=lambda k: per_layer[k]["val_acc"])
        best_metrics = per_layer[best_L]

        print(f"  Best layer: {best_L}")
        print(f"  Best layer train accuracy: {best_metrics['train_acc']:.4f}")
        print(f"  Best layer validation accuracy: {best_metrics['val_acc']:.4f}")
        print(
            f"  Best layer random-direction validation accuracy: {best_metrics['random_acc']:.4f}"
        )
        print(
            f"  Best layer shuffled-labels validation accuracy: {best_metrics['shuffled_acc']:.4f}"
        )
        print(f"  Best layer direction norm: {best_metrics['direction_norm']:.4f}")

        # Compute best train/val loss (1 - acc)
        train_losses = [(L, 1.0 - per_layer[L]["train_acc"]) for L in per_layer]
        val_losses = [(L, 1.0 - per_layer[L]["val_acc"]) for L in per_layer]
        best_train_loss_layer, best_train_loss = min(train_losses, key=lambda x: x[1])
        best_val_loss_layer, best_val_loss = min(val_losses, key=lambda x: x[1])

        print(
            f"  Best train loss (layer {best_train_loss_layer}): {best_train_loss:.4f}"
        )
        print(
            f"  Best validation loss (layer {best_val_loss_layer}): {best_val_loss:.4f}"
        )

    if best_probe_acc is not None:
        print(f"  Harmfulness direction probe accuracy (best): {best_probe_acc:.4f}")

    # Compute test F1 from predictions/ground_truth
    preds = data.get("predictions", [])
    gts = data.get("ground_truth", [])
    if preds and gts:
        preds = np.array(preds)
        gts = np.array(gts)
        tp = int(((preds == 1) & (gts == 1)).sum())
        fp = int(((preds == 1) & (gts == 0)).sum())
        fn = int(((preds == 0) & (gts == 1)).sum())
        tn = int(((preds == 0) & (gts == 0)).sum())
        precision = tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) > 0 else 0.0
        recall = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0
        f1 = (
            2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
            if (precision + recall) > 0
            else 0.0
        )
        test_acc = (tp + tn) / len(preds)
        print(f"  Test accuracy (best layer): {test_acc:.4f}")
        print(f"  Test precision (best layer): {precision:.4f}")
        print(f"  Test recall (best layer): {recall:.4f}")
        print(f"  Test F1 score (best layer): {f1:.4f}")

plot_analyses.analysis: This appears to be a confusion matrix for a Latent Guard classifier evaluated on a jailbreak detection task. The matrix shows perfect classification: 40 true negatives (benign correctly identified) and 40 true positives (harmful correctly identified), with zero false positives and zero false negatives. This 100% accuracy result on a small balanced test set (80 samples) suggests the linear probe on the harmfulness direction is extracting a highly separable signal. However, such perfect performance is suspicious and may indicate: (1) the evaluation set is too small or too easy, (2) potential data leakage between training and test sets, or (3) the harmful/benign contrast is too clean (e.g., simple AdvBench vs Alpaca contrast without adversarial examples). For a rigorous evaluation supporting the paper's central claim about Latent Guard matching Llama Guard 3, this needs to be validated on harder benchmarks (JailbreakBench, XSTest for over-refusal) and with actual jailbreak attempts.

This plot shows cosine similarity between the harmfulness direction and refusal direction across transformer layers (0-31) for Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Key observations: (1) At early layers (0-5), similarity is near zero or slightly negative, indicating the directions are essentially orthogonal in early representations. (2) There is a sharp transition around layers 6-10 where similarity rises steeply. (3) From layers 10-31, the two directions become highly aligned with cosine similarity around 0.7-0.85, peaking near 0.85 at middle-to-late layers. This is a critical finding for the paper's hypothesis: while the paper claims the two concepts are 'separable linear directions,' the high cosine similarity (>0.7) in most layers suggests they are NOT well-separated in the residual stream — they largely co-vary. This partially undermines the separability claim and suggests the authors need to either (a) identify specific layers where separation is highest for steering experiments, or (b) use orthogonalization/projection methods to isolate the components. The early layers (0-5) may be where true separation exists but these layers typically don't encode high-level semantic concepts well.

This plot shows probe accuracy for harmfulness classification across layers 0-31. The accuracy starts near 0.5 (chance) at layer 0, rises rapidly through layers 1-5, and reaches near-perfect accuracy (~1.0) by layer 5-6, remaining at ceiling for all subsequent layers (6-31). This is consistent with prior literature (Zou et al., Arditi et al.) showing that harmfulness/refusal concepts emerge in early-to-middle layers of instruction-tuned LLMs. The result validates that a linear probe can reliably decode harmfulness from residual stream activations. However, the ceiling effect starting so early (layer 5) means the probe can't discriminate between layers for choosing the 'best' harmfulness direction — all middle/late layers work equally well by this metric. Combined with the previous plot showing high cosine similarity with refusal, this suggests the probe may actually be picking up a mixed harmfulness+refusal signal rather than pure harmfulness. Additional validation (e.g., testing on jailbroken prompts where the model complies with harmful requests) would be needed to disentangle these.

This plot shows refusal probe accuracy across layers 0-31. The curve shows: (1) chance performance at layer 0 (~0.5), (2) a gradual rise from layers 1-4, (3) reaching ~1.0 accuracy by layer 5, (4) a slight dip around layers 6-9 (down to ~0.95), and (5) full ceiling accuracy from layer 10 onward. The pattern is very similar to the harmfulness probe accuracy, which is expected given the high cosine similarity between the two directions shown in the earlier plot. The refusal signal appears to be linearly decodable from very early layers, consistent with prior findings that refusal has a strong linear representation. The near-identical accuracy curves for both harmfulness and refusal probes, combined with their high cosine similarity, reinforces the concern that these two directions may not be as separable as the hypothesis claims — the probes may be detecting largely the same underlying representation. Future experiments should test whether the two directions can be used to independently steer behavior (e.g., steering on harmfulness while keeping refusal constant, and vice versa) as originally proposed in the hypothesis.

This plot displays token position for the two directions across layers 0-31. Both harmfulness (blue) and refusal (orange) directions are consistently located at token position -1 (the final token) across ALL layers. This contradicts a key claim in the research hypothesis, which states that 'the harmfulness judgment is written at the final instruction-token position, while the decision to refuse is committed just after the instruction, immediately before the response begins.' The experiment appears to only be extracting directions at a single fixed token position (-1) rather than exploring multiple positions to find the optimal one for each concept. To properly test the hypothesis about differential token positions, the pipeline needs to be modified to: (1) sweep over multiple token positions (e.g., last instruction token, chat template tokens, first response token position), (2) measure probe accuracy or steering effect at each position, and (3) demonstrate that harmfulness is best decoded at one position and refusal at another. As currently shown, this plot provides no evidence for the token-position separation hypothesis.

This plot shows attack success rate (ASR) versus steering strength (alpha ranging from -3 to +3) for harmfulness direction steering. Key observations: (1) At alpha=0 (no steering), baseline ASR is ~0.06 (6%), indicating the model refuses most harmful prompts by default. (2) For negative alpha (-3 to -1), ASR remains near baseline (~0-0.1). (3) At alpha=+1, ASR jumps dramatically to 0.7. (4) At alpha=+2 and +3, ASR reaches ~1.0 (100% attack success). This monotonic increase demonstrates that adding the harmfulness direction to activations effectively jailbreaks the model, causing it to comply with harmful requests. However, this result is somewhat problematic for the paper's core hypothesis: if steering along the 'harmfulness' direction increases compliance (i.e., reduces refusal), then this direction is behaving like a refusal-suppression direction, not a pure harmfulness-perception direction. Under the hypothesis, moving along the harmfulness axis should 'flip the model's internal judgment of whether an input is harmful, independent of whether it refuses.' The observed strong effect on refusal behavior suggests the extracted direction is entangled with refusal — consistent with the high cosine similarity (~0.8) shown earlier. To properly demonstrate dissociation, the authors need to show steering that changes internal harmfulness judgment (measurable via probes) WITHOUT changing refusal behavior, which this plot does not show.

nodes.vlm_feedback_summary: The plots show preliminary implementation results for the paper's hypothesis that harmfulness and refusal are separable linear directions in Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Key findings: (1) Both harmfulness and refusal probes achieve near-perfect classification accuracy from early layers (~layer 5) onward. (2) A Latent Guard classifier achieves perfect 100% accuracy on an 80-sample balanced test set, though this needs harder benchmarks for validation. (3) Steering along the 'harmfulness' direction dramatically increases attack success rate (from 6% to 100% at alpha=+2), demonstrating strong behavioral effect. HOWEVER, the results raise significant concerns about the core separability hypothesis: (a) The cosine similarity between harmfulness and refusal directions is very high (~0.7-0.85) across most layers, suggesting they are NOT well-separated in the residual stream. (b) The token position analysis shows both directions extracted at the same position (-1) across all layers, providing no evidence for the paper's claim of differential token positions for the two concepts. (c) The strong effect of 'harmfulness' steering on refusal behavior (jailbreaking) suggests the extracted direction is entangled with refusal rather than being a pure harmfulness-perception axis. The implementation successfully extracts and steers with directions, but the current experimental design does not yet demonstrate the key dissociation claims. Recommendations: sweep multiple token positions, orthogonalize the directions, and test steering effects on internal probe predictions independently of behavioral refusal.

Hyperparam tuning name: N_PER_CLASS (number of training prompts per class).
I'll implement a hyperparameter sweep over N_PER_CLASS ∈ {100, 200, 400, 500}, capped by available dataset size. For each value, I'll extract activations for that number of prompts per class, train the diff-of-means + logistic regression probe across the same layers, and pick the best (N_PER_CLASS, layer) combination based on validation accuracy. Results are stored in the required nested dict structure and saved to experiment_data.npy.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import os

working_dir = os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "working")

try:
    experiment_data = np.load(
        os.path.join(working_dir, "experiment_data.npy"), allow_pickle=True
    ).item()
    ed = experiment_data["N_PER_CLASS_tuning"]["llama3_advbench_alpaca"]
    N_candidates = ed["N_candidates"]
    per_config = ed["per_config"]
    best_N = ed["best_N"]
    best_layer = ed["best_layer"]
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error loading experiment data: {e}")
    ed = None

# Plot 1: Val accuracy per layer for each N
try:
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    for N in N_candidates:
        layers = sorted(per_config[N]["per_layer"].keys())
        vals = [per_config[N]["per_layer"][L]["val_acc"] for L in layers]
        plt.plot(layers, vals, "o-", label=f"N={N}")
    plt.xlabel("Layer")
    plt.ylabel("Validation Accuracy")
    plt.title(
        "Llama3 AdvBench/Alpaca: Probe Val Accuracy vs Layer\nSweep over N_PER_CLASS"
    )
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, "llama3_advbench_alpaca_val_acc_per_layer.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot1: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 2: Train vs Val accuracy for best N
try:
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    layers = sorted(per_config[best_N]["per_layer"].keys())
    tr = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["train_acc"] for L in layers]
    va = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["val_acc"] for L in layers]
    plt.plot(layers, tr, "o-", label="Train Acc")
    plt.plot(layers, va, "s-", label="Val Acc")
    plt.xlabel("Layer")
    plt.ylabel("Accuracy")
    plt.title(
        f"Llama3 AdvBench/Alpaca: Train vs Val Accuracy (N={best_N})\nBest layer={best_layer}"
    )
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, "llama3_advbench_alpaca_train_vs_val_bestN.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot2: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 3: Baselines comparison at best N
try:
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    layers = sorted(per_config[best_N]["per_layer"].keys())
    va = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["val_acc"] for L in layers]
    ra = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["random_acc"] for L in layers]
    sa = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["shuffled_acc"] for L in layers]
    plt.plot(layers, va, "o-", label="Mean-diff direction")
    plt.plot(layers, ra, "s--", label="Random direction")
    plt.plot(layers, sa, "^--", label="Shuffled labels")
    plt.xlabel("Layer")
    plt.ylabel("Validation Accuracy")
    plt.title(
        f"Llama3 AdvBench/Alpaca: Probe vs Baselines (N={best_N})\nHarmfulness direction probe"
    )
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, "llama3_advbench_alpaca_baselines_bestN.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot3: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 4: Best val acc per N
try:
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
    best_vals = [per_config[N]["best_val_acc"] for N in N_candidates]
    best_layers = [per_config[N]["best_layer"] for N in N_candidates]
    plt.plot(N_candidates, best_vals, "o-")
    for N, v, L in zip(N_candidates, best_vals, best_layers):
        plt.annotate(f"L={L}", (N, v), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(5, 5))
    plt.xlabel("N per class")
    plt.ylabel("Best Val Accuracy")
    plt.title(
        "Llama3 AdvBench/Alpaca: Best Val Accuracy vs N_PER_CLASS\n(Layer annotated per point)"
    )
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, "llama3_advbench_alpaca_bestacc_vs_N.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot4: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 5: Confusion matrix for best config
try:
    preds = np.array(ed["predictions"])
    gt = np.array(ed["ground_truth"])
    cm = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    for t, p in zip(gt, preds):
        cm[int(t), int(p)] += 1
    plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
    plt.imshow(cm, cmap="Blues")
    plt.colorbar()
    for i in range(2):
        for j in range(2):
            plt.text(j, i, str(cm[i, j]), ha="center", va="center", color="black")
    plt.xticks([0, 1], ["Benign", "Harmful"])
    plt.yticks([0, 1], ["Benign", "Harmful"])
    plt.xlabel("Predicted")
    plt.ylabel("Ground Truth")
    plt.title(
        f"Llama3 AdvBench/Alpaca: Confusion Matrix\nBest config (N={best_N}, layer={best_layer})"
    )
    plt.savefig(
        os.path.join(working_dir, "llama3_advbench_alpaca_confusion_matrix.png"),
        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot5: {e}")
    plt.close()

try:
    print(
        f"Best N={ed['best_N']}, Best layer={ed['best_layer']}, Val Acc={ed['harmfulness_direction_probe_accuracy']:.4f}"
    )
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error printing metric: {e}")

This inverted pattern is unusual and suggests either (a) the model is being evaluated but not truly trained on this dataset, (b) there is a labeling or evaluation issue, or (c) the model is a pretrained one being tested in some transfer setting. This does not correspond to the LLM research idea about harmfulness/refusal directions.

Imagenette accuracy curves show train accuracy climbing from ~25% to ~55% and validation accuracy from ~35% to ~65% over 15 epochs. Interestingly, validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy throughout, which can occur with heavy training-time regularization (e.g., dropout, augmentation) or a small/easier validation split. This is still an image classification task unrelated to the stated LLM safety research direction.

Combined loss curves across the four datasets (fashion_mnist, dtd, imagenet-val, imagenette) show varying loss dynamics: fashion_mnist and imagenette losses decrease steadily indicating learning; DTD loss decreases sharply on training but likely reflects the overfitting seen in accuracy; imagenet-val loss remains relatively flat/high.     plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    for N in N_candidates:
        layers = sorted(per_config[N]["per_layer"].keys())
        vals = [per_config[N]["per_layer"][L]["val_acc"] for L in layers]

    plt.ylabel("Validation Accuracy")
    plt.title(

        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot1: {e}")
    plt.close()

    plt.grid(True)

        bbox_inches="tight",
    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot2: {e}")
    plt.close()

try:
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    layers = sorted(per_config[best_N]["per_layer"].keys())
    va = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["val_acc"] for L in layers]
    ra = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["random_acc"] for L in layers]
    sa = [per_config[best_N]["per_layer"][L]["shuffled_acc"] for L in layers]
    plt.plot(layers, va, "o-", label="Mean-diff direction")

    plt.ylabel("Validation Accuracy")

    )
    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot3: {e}")
    plt.close()

    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
    best_vals = [per_config[N]["best_val_acc"] for N in N_candidates]

    plt.close()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error creating plot4: {e}")
    plt.close()

# Plot 5: Confusion matrix for best config
try:
    preds = np.array(ed["predictions"])
    gt = np.array(ed["ground_truth"])

    n = arr.shape[axis]
    if n <= 1:
        return np.zeros(arr.shape[1:]) if arr.ndim > 1 else 0.0
    return np.std(arr, axis=axis, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)

try:
    cm = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=float)

    for ed in eds:

        run_cm = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)

            run_cm[int(t), int(p)] += 1
        per_run_cms.append(run_cm)
        cm += run_cm
    per_run_cms = np.array(per_run_cms, dtype=float)
    mean_cm = per_run_cms.mean(axis=0)
